triage.name: Reflux in Infants
triage.reason: Very common infant presentation of spitting up and irritability, diagnosed clinically with attention to warning signs.

demographics: Affects infants of all races and ethnicities equally
Most common in the first few months of life; improves as the lower esophageal sphincter matures

risk_factors.text: Neurologic impairment such as cerebral palsy
Chronic lung disease such as cystic fibrosis

comorbidities: Congenital esophageal anomalies repaired in infancy
family_history: Family history of gastroesophageal reflux disease

chief_complaints.text: My baby spits up after almost every feeding
My baby cries and arches her back during and after feeds
My baby seems fussy and uncomfortable after eating

hpi.onset: Gradual, starting in the first weeks to months of life
hpi.duration: Weeks to months; typically resolves by 12–14 months of age
hpi.progression: Spitting up is frequent in early infancy, peaks around 4 months, then gradually improves as the baby grows and starts sitting upright; symptoms that persist or worsen after 12–18 months are unusual
hpi.location: Chest and upper abdomen; parents describe milk coming up into the mouth
hpi.quality: Effortless regurgitation of milk, sometimes with arching of the back and crying
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate in most infants; severe when it interferes with feeding, sleep, or growth
hpi.timing: Occurs during or shortly after feedings; may also happen when the baby is lying flat or straining
relieving: Holding the baby upright after feeds

associated_symptoms.text: Arching of the back during or right after eating
Poor feeding or refusing to eat

pertinent_negatives: Vomiting that begins after 6 months of age
Failure to thrive or weight loss
Symptoms that started suddenly in a previously well infant

atypical.how_it_differs: Premature infants and those with neurologic impairment may present with feeding intolerance, apnea, or bradycardia rather than obvious spitting up; symptoms may persist longer and be more severe.
Older infants and toddlers may present with irritability, poor appetite, or respiratory symptoms rather than visible spitting up; symptoms that persist beyond 18 months suggest a different diagnosis.

general.mild: Well-appearing, thriving infant; happy and interactive between feeds; normal tone and hydration
general.moderate: Mildly fussy or irritable, especially after feeds; otherwise well-appearing and adequately hydrated
general.severe: Irritable or inconsolable with feeds, arching and back extension; may look uncomfortable or undernourished
general.critical: Ill-appearing, lethargic or inconsolable, signs of dehydration or poor perfusion; poor responsiveness

findings.maneuver: Measure weight, length and head circumference and plot on the WHO/CDC growth chart
findings.finding: Weight and length tracking along a normal percentile curve

findings.maneuver: Measure weight and compare with prior weights and expected growth velocity
findings.finding: Weight crossing downward across percentiles or weight loss, suggesting inadequate intake

findings.maneuver: Assess mucous membranes, skin turgor, anterior fontanelle, tears and capillary refill
findings.finding: Dry mucous membranes, sunken fontanelle, decreased skin turgor or delayed capillary refill

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen with a warm hand, starting away from any tender area
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender, non-distended abdomen without mass or organomegaly

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant and epigastrium for a mass
findings.finding: Firm, olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant (suggests pyloric stenosis)

findings.maneuver: Observe the abdomen while the infant is calm and feeding
findings.finding: Visible gastric waves passing left to right (suggests pyloric stenosis or obstruction)

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields and observe respiratory effort
findings.finding: Clear breath sounds, no wheeze, stridor or increased work of breathing

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the chest after a feed
findings.finding: Wheeze, crackles or transmitted upper airway sounds suggesting aspiration or reactive airway disease

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and palpate peripheral pulses
findings.finding: Normal S1/S2, no murmur, regular rate and rhythm, strong symmetric pulses

findings.maneuver: Assess tone, posture, primitive reflexes and level of alertness
findings.finding: Age-appropriate tone, reflexes and alertness without focal deficits

findings.maneuver: Assess tone and posture during handling
findings.finding: Hyper- or hypotonia, opisthotonus or delayed milestones suggesting an underlying neurologic disorder

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx, ears and nose; palpate the anterior fontanelle
findings.finding: Normal oropharynx without lesions, flat fontanelle, no drooling or pooling of secretions

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin for color, perfusion and rashes
findings.finding: Warm, well-perfused skin without jaundice, petechiae or eczematous changes

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected anatomic abnormality such as malrotation, pyloric stenosis, or hiatal hernia

findings.text: Normal position of the duodenojejunal junction in the left upper quadrant, excluding malrotation
Free gastroesophageal reflux of contrast into the distal esophagus
Normal-caliber pylorus with normal gastric emptying
Hiatal hernia with part of the stomach above the diaphragm

imaging.study: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with esophageal biopsy
imaging.preferred_when: Persistent symptoms despite treatment, suspected esophagitis, or concern for eosinophilic esophagitis

findings.text: Erythema, erosions, or linear streaks in the distal esophagus (esophagitis)
Esophageal biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration consistent with eosinophilic esophagitis
Esophageal biopsy showing basal cell hyperplasia and elongated papillae consistent with reflux

imaging.preferred_when: Unclear relationship between symptoms and reflux, or before considering surgery

findings.text: Increased number of acid reflux episodes over 24 hours
Positive symptom correlation between reflux events and crying or arching

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pyloric stenosis or other structural cause

findings.text: Normal pylorus with no thickening or elongation
Thickened and elongated pylorus consistent with pyloric stenosis

initial.why: Assesses for anemia or infection if poor feeding, vomiting, or failure to thrive is present
initial.only_if: poor weight gain, vomiting, or concern for infection

initial.why: Evaluates electrolytes and hydration if vomiting is frequent or severe
initial.only_if: frequent vomiting, dehydration, or poor intake

supporting.why: Evaluates for anatomic abnormalities such as malrotation or pyloric stenosis when warning signs are present
supporting.only_if: bilious vomiting, projectile vomiting, or suspected structural abnormality

supporting.test: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with esophageal biopsy
supporting.why: Directly visualizes and biopsies the esophagus when esophagitis or eosinophilic esophagitis is suspected
supporting.only_if: persistent symptoms despite treatment or suspected esophagitis

supporting.why: Quantifies acid exposure and correlates symptoms with reflux episodes
supporting.only_if: diagnosis remains unclear or surgery is being considered

supporting.why: Rules out pyloric stenosis when projectile vomiting is present
supporting.only_if: projectile vomiting or suspected pyloric stenosis

not_indicated.why: Not needed for typical uncomplicated reflux, which is a clinical diagnosis

not_indicated.test: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with esophageal biopsy
not_indicated.why: Invasive and not routine for uncomplicated reflux
Reserved for atypical or refractory cases, not routine diagnosis
Not indicated unless pyloric stenosis or another structural cause is suspected
Not routinely needed for uncomplicated reflux
Not routinely needed for uncomplicated reflux

decision_points: Diagnose typical reflux clinically; testing only if warning signs or poor response to feeding changes
Warning signs (bilious vomiting, projectile vomiting, hematemesis, failure to thrive, onset after 6 months) prompt imaging or endoscopy
Consider pyloric stenosis in a 3–6 week old with projectile nonbilious vomiting and order ultrasound

differential.name: Pyloric stenosis
differential.why_considered: Nonbilious vomiting in a young infant can be mistaken for reflux
differential.trigger: Projectile, forceful nonbilious vomiting in a 3–6 week old, hungry after vomiting, with poor weight gain

history: Vomiting becomes projectile and increasingly forceful
Infant remains hungry and feeds eagerly after vomiting
Progressive rather than improving over time
exam: Palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant
Signs of dehydration and weight loss
labs: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with low chloride
imaging: Abdominal ultrasound showing thickened and elongated pylorus
Upper GI series with a string sign or double-track sign

differential.name: Malrotation with midgut volvulus
differential.why_considered: Vomiting in an infant can be attributed to reflux when the true cause is a surgical emergency
differential.trigger: Bilious (green) vomiting, especially with acute onset, abdominal distension, or lethargy

history: Sudden onset in a previously well infant
exam: Signs of shock or poor perfusion
imaging: Upper GI series showing abnormal duodenojejunal junction position or corkscrew appearance
Abdominal ultrasound showing abnormal SMA/SMV relationship or whirlpool sign

differential.name: Eosinophilic esophagitis
differential.why_considered: Feeding difficulty, irritability, and vomiting in an infant can mimic reflux

history: Personal or family history of atopy, asthma, or eczema
exam: Signs of atopic disease such as eczema
imaging: Esophageal biopsy showing dense eosinophilic infiltration (≥15 eosinophils per high-power field)
Endoscopy may show furrows, rings, or white exudates

differential.name: Cow's milk protein allergy
differential.why_considered: Vomiting, irritability, and poor feeding in a formula-fed or breastfed infant can resemble reflux

history: Symptoms worsen with cow's milk formula or maternal dairy intake
imaging: Endoscopy with biopsy may show eosinophilic inflammation if performed

differential.name: Laryngomalacia
differential.why_considered: Noisy breathing, coughing, and feeding difficulty can be attributed to reflux

history: Inspiratory stridor that worsens when supine or crying
Symptoms present from birth or early weeks
Feeding difficulty with choking or cyanotic spells
exam: Worsening of stridor with neck flexion or agitation
imaging: Flexible laryngoscopy showing omega-shaped epiglottis and prolapsing arytenoids

differential.name: Gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Vomiting and irritability in an infant can be mistaken for reflux

history: Acute onset of vomiting and diarrhea

differential.name: Increased intracranial pressure
differential.why_considered: Vomiting and irritability in an infant can be attributed to reflux when a neurologic cause is present
differential.trigger: Vomiting with lethargy, bulging fontanelle, abnormal tone, or seizures

exam: Sunsetting eyes or cranial nerve abnormalities
imaging: Head ultrasound or CT/MRI showing ventricular dilation or mass

severity.mild: Frequent effortless spitting up in a thriving, well-appearing infant; no feeding or growth problems
severity.moderate: Spitting up with irritability, arching, or feeding refusal; weight gain may be slower but still adequate
severity.severe: Poor weight gain or weight loss, significant feeding difficulty, respiratory symptoms such as coughing or wheezing, or esophagitis
severity.critical: Signs of dehydration, lethargy, apnea, or aspiration with respiratory compromise

red_flags.meaning: Suggests intestinal obstruction or malrotation with volvulus; requires urgent evaluation
Suggests pyloric stenosis or increased intracranial pressure

red_flags.finding: Blood in vomit or bloody stools
red_flags.meaning: Suggests esophagitis, gastritis, or a bleeding disorder

red_flags.finding: Failure to thrive or weight loss
red_flags.meaning: Inadequate intake or malabsorption; needs further workup
Unusual for typical reflux; consider other diagnoses
Suggests aspiration or severe respiratory involvement

special_populations.differences: Premature infants and those with neurologic impairment may present with feeding intolerance, apnea, or bradycardia rather than obvious spitting up; symptoms may persist longer and be more severe.
Older infants and toddlers may present with irritability, poor appetite, or respiratory symptoms rather than visible spitting up; symptoms that persist beyond 18 months suggest a different diagnosis.

key_questions.question: What does the spit-up look like, and how forceful is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Effortless, nonbilious regurgitation of milk; projectile or bilious vomiting points to pyloric stenosis or obstruction

key_questions.question: When does the spitting up happen relative to feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: During or shortly after feeds, worse when lying flat or straining

key_questions.question: How old was your baby when this started, and is it getting better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset in the first weeks to months of life with gradual improvement; onset after 6 months or progressive worsening is unusual

key_questions.question: Is your baby gaining weight and having normal wet diapers?
key_questions.looking_for: Adequate weight gain along the growth curve and normal urine output; poor weight gain or weight loss suggests GERD or another cause

key_questions.question: Does your baby arch her back, cry, or seem uncomfortable during or after feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Arching, irritability, or crying after eating suggesting esophagitis or discomfort

key_questions.question: Does your baby cough, choke, gag, or wheeze with feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Respiratory symptoms suggesting aspiration or airway involvement

key_questions.question: How much and how often are you feeding, and do you burp during feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Overfeeding or large-volume feeds that worsen reflux; opportunities for feeding changes

key_questions.question: What have you tried so far, such as holding upright, smaller feeds, or thickened feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Response to conservative feeding measures before considering medication

key_questions.question: Was your baby born early, or does she have any neurologic or lung conditions?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity, cerebral palsy, cystic fibrosis, hiatal hernia, or prior esophageal surgery

key_questions.question: Is there any blood or green color in the vomit, or blood in the stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilious or bloody emesis or bloody stools, which suggest obstruction, esophagitis, or a bleeding source

key_questions.question: Has your baby had spells of stopping breathing, turning blue, or becoming limp?
key_questions.looking_for: Apnea, cyanotic spells, or apparent life-threatening events suggesting aspiration or severe disease

key_questions.question: Is your baby lethargic, difficult to wake, or having seizures?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurologic warning signs such as lethargy, poor responsiveness, or seizures

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have reflux or food allergies?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of gastroesophageal reflux disease or atopy

key_questions.question: Does anyone smoke around the baby?
key_questions.looking_for: Secondhand tobacco smoke exposure that can worsen reflux symptoms

reasoning_points: Effortless, nonbilious regurgitation during or shortly after feeds in a thriving infant
Onset in the first weeks to months of life with gradual improvement as the lower esophageal sphincter matures
Symptoms worse when lying flat or straining and relieved by upright positioning, burping, and smaller feeds
Irritability, back arching, or feeding refusal suggesting discomfort or esophagitis
Normal growth and hydration with a soft, non-tender abdomen and no warning signs
Warning signs such as bilious or projectile vomiting, hematemesis, failure to thrive, onset after 6 months, apnea, or lethargy prompt further evaluation
Typical reflux is a clinical diagnosis; testing is reserved for atypical or refractory cases

easy: Healthy 2-month-old with frequent effortless spit-up after feeds
Happy, thriving infant with normal weight gain and a soft abdomen
Symptoms improve with upright positioning and smaller, more frequent feeds
No warning signs such as bilious or projectile vomiting
medium: Infant with irritability and back arching after feeds but still gaining weight
Formula-fed infant with vomiting and eczema raising concern for cow's milk protein allergy
Premature infant with feeding intolerance and slower weight gain
Symptoms persisting beyond 12 months requiring consideration of other diagnoses
hard: 3–6 week old with projectile nonbilious vomiting and an olive-shaped mass suggesting pyloric stenosis
Infant with bilious vomiting and lethargy suggesting malrotation with volvulus
Infant with apnea or cyanotic spells suggesting aspiration or an apparent life-threatening event
Infant with vomiting, lethargy, and a bulging fontanelle suggesting increased intracranial pressure
Infant with feeding refusal and poor response to acid suppression suggesting eosinophilic esophagitis
